# TLS and the dependency policy for the Rust core

Research date: 2026-09-29, continued 2026-09-30 (second run verified the open items from the first run, corrected the ALPN ordering claim, and added section 8 on HTTP/3 and QUIC at the owner's request). Every claim below is tied to a fetched source (listed at the end) or to a measurement run on this machine (`measure-cargo-tree.txt` in this directory). Anything else is marked unverified.

## 2. Is a zero-third-party-crate policy feasible for a TLS-terminating server?

No. The reasons, from the sources:

- Writing TLS 1.3 plus X.509 path validation plus AEAD, ECDHE, and signature primitives in house would recreate exactly the surface that took the rustls project a decade and external funding to harden. The project's own retrospective says the CNCF-funded Cure53 audit was arranged between 2018 and 2020 and that ISRG's Prossimo later "funded myself, @cpu, @djc and others to dramatically improve the pace and depth of development" and delivered "pluggable cryptography providers, no_std support, FIPS certification, post-quantum key exchange and Encrypted ClientHello" (rustls.dev, A Decade of Rustls).
- rustls ships security fixes with a defined process: "Security fixes are backported only to versions released within the last 2 years", advisories go to RustSec, and the project fuzzes with `cargo fuzz` and OSS-Fuzz (rustls SECURITY.md). The advisory cadence is real: RUSTSEC-2026-0285 (rustls <0.23.45, 2026-09-14, "TLS 1.3 handshake messages incorrectly accepted across encryption level boundaries", CVSS 5.3) and RUSTSEC-2026-0049 (rustls-webpki <0.103.10, 2026-03-20, CRL distribution point matching). An in-house stack would have neither the advisory pipeline nor the fuzz corpus.
- Cryptography needs native code for constant time and speed. Both first-party providers are C plus assembly behind a Rust API: ring's C and assembly "comes from BoringSSL" (ring README); aws-lc-rs binds AWS-LC, which "is based on code from the Google BoringSSL project and the OpenSSL project" and carries HOL Light proofs for its s2n-bignum assembly (AWS-LC README). The pure-Rust alternative, graviola, also embeds "assembler routines from the s2n-bignum project" and says "This project is very new, so exercise due caution" (graviola README).

The policy that is feasible: zero third-party crates in every crate that does not terminate TLS (HTTP parsing, routing, codecs, ORM wire protocols, the no_std core), and one explicitly vetted, pinned, deny-enforced set for the TLS crate and the async I/O boundary.

### The measured minimum set (rustls 0.23.45 resolved on 2026-09-29, `cargo tree -e normal,build`, duplicates from `(*)` markers removed)

| Configuration | Unique crates | Members |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rustls + `ring`, no `std` (the smallest TLS engine) | 14 | rustls, rustls-webpki 0.103.15, rustls-pki-types 1.15.1, ring 0.17.14, untrusted, subtle, zeroize, once_cell, getrandom 0.2, libc, cfg-if; build: cc, shlex, find-msvc-tools |
| rustls + `ring` + `std` + `tls12` + tokio-rustls 0.26.6 (Linux) | 17 | the above plus tokio 1.53.1, pin-project-lite, tokio-rustls |
| rustls + `aws_lc_rs` + `std` + `tls12` + tokio-rustls (Linux or Windows) | 21 | rustls, rustls-webpki, rustls-pki-types, aws-lc-rs 1.18.1, aws-lc-sys 0.45.0, untrusted, subtle, zeroize, once_cell, getrandom 0.4, cfg-if, tokio, pin-project-lite, tokio-rustls; build: cc, cmake, dunce, fs_extra, jobserver, shlex, find-msvc-tools |
| same, normal edges only (what links into the binary) | 12 | no build-script helpers |

aws-lc-sys 0.45.0 is 67.0 MB of packaged source ("Source code size: 67.0 MB", docs.rs crate page). ring's crate description on crates.io is literally "An experiment." and its README repeats BoringSSL's warning that it "is not intended for general use" and points to SIDE-CHANNELS.md for mitigation limits.

Binding footprints measured the same way (Linux target): `napi 3.13.0` with `default-features = false, features = ["napi6"]` plus napi-derive and napi-build resolves to 32 unique crates, most of them the proc-macro toolchain (syn 2 and 3, quote, proc-macro2) and `futures`; `pyo3 0.29.2` with `abi3-py310` resolves to 13 unique crates (pyo3, pyo3-ffi, pyo3-build-config, pyo3-macros, pyo3-macros-backend, libc, once_cell, target-lexicon, heck, unicode-ident, syn, quote, proc-macro2). With napi's default features on, docs.rs lists direct dependencies including anyhow, chrono, serde, serde_json, tokio, tokio-stream, tracing, and encoding_rs, so the pamoja choice of `default-features = false` is the right baseline.

## 3. rustls facts that shape the design

Version and license: rustls 0.23.45 resolved today; "Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT" (docs.rs). rustls-pki-types is "MIT OR Apache-2.0"; tokio-rustls "MIT OR Apache-2.0"; rustls-native-certs "Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT"; webpki-roots 1.0.9 is CDLA-Permissive-2.0 (not in the pamoja allowlist, and a server does not need it unless it verifies clients or dials upstream with a bundled root set). From the crates.io API (2026-09-30): rustls-webpki is `ISC` (newest 0.103.15, max 0.104.0-alpha.7); ring 0.17.14 is `Apache-2.0 AND ISC`; aws-lc-sys 0.45.0 is the compound expression `ISC AND (Apache-2.0 OR ISC) AND Apache-2.0 AND MIT AND BSD-3-Clause AND (Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT) AND (Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT-0)`. Every AND term of that expression is satisfiable from pamoja's existing allow list (ISC, Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD-3-Clause), so the provider needs no license exception in `deny.toml`; the same holds for ring.

Protocol features (rustls manual, Features): implemented are TLS 1.2 and 1.3, ECDSA/Ed25519/RSA server auth, ECDHE forward secrecy, "Post-quantum hybrid key exchange with X25519MLKEM768", AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, ALPN, SNI, TLS 1.2 resumption by IDs and tickets, "TLS1.3 resumption via tickets or session storage", "TLS1.3 0-RTT data", server and optional client authentication, extended master secret, "OCSP stapling by servers", and certificate compression. Deliberately absent: SSL and TLS 1.0/1.1, RC4, DES/3DES, EXPORT and MAC-then-encrypt suites, suites without forward secrecy, renegotiation, Kerberos, TLS 1.2 compression, "Discrete-log Diffie-Hellman", automatic version downgrade. This means rustls cannot be misconfigured into most of what RFC 9325 forbids.

Crate features (docs.rs features page for 0.23.45): `default = aws_lc_rs, logging, prefer-post-quantum, std, tls12`; `std` turns on "once_cell, pki-types, and webpki std features"; `ring`; `fips` enables "aws-lc-rs fips and webpki aws-lc-rs-fips"; `brotli` and `zlib` add RFC 8879 compression crates; `custom-provider` "disables implicit use of built-in providers"; `hashbrown` for no_std session caches; `read_buf` (nightly). The `tls12` feature "cannot be reliably disabled if other dependencies require it" because features are additive (docs.rs lib page). MSRV: the docs.rs lib page says "Rustls requires Rust 1.71 or later" while SECURITY.md says the MSRV "will be no more recent than 9 versions old, or approximately 12 months" and is "Currently set at Rust 1.85"; treat 1.85 as the operative floor for 0.23.45 and the lib-page number as stale.

Future direction: "In 0.24, providers are separate crates, such as rustls-aws-lc-rs and rustls-ring, and the main rustls crate no longer has crate features for selecting a provider" (rustls.dev blog). The README already lists `rustls-aws-lc-rs` and `rustls-ring` as the first-party providers. The allowlist below names both spellings so the 0.24 move is a version bump, not a policy change.

no_std: the crate is `#![no_std]` internally; the `std` feature enables "the high-level (buffered) Connection API and other functionality which relies on the std library". Without `std`: `ServerConfig::builder()` and `builder_with_provider()` are std-only, and "This API must be used by no_std users": `ServerConfig::builder_with_details(provider: Arc<CryptoProvider>, time_provider: Arc<dyn TimeProvider>)`. `DefaultTimeProvider` is std-only; `TimeProvider::current_time(&self) -> Option<UnixTime>` exists to "check if a certificate has expired during certificate validation, or to check the age of a ticket". The unbuffered API "does not make use of the std::io::Read and std::io::Write traits so it's usable in no-std context" and is "built around a state machine interface where the API user must handle each state", with the caller owning every buffer. Session storage under no_std: "the default is to not store any sessions. In a no-std context, by enabling the hashbrown feature you may provide your own session_storage using ServerSessionMemoryCache and a crate::lock::MakeMutex implementation". `Ticketer::new()` and `TicketRotator` are std-only. The provider constraint decides it: aws-lc-rs "requires the std library. We currently do not support a #![no_std] build" (aws-lc-rs docs), while ring supports `os = "none"` targets through `less-safe-getrandom-custom-or-rdrand` and wasm through `wasm32_unknown_unknown_js`. So a no_std TLS build means ring (or graviola, or a custom provider) plus the unbuffered API plus a caller-supplied clock and lock.

FIPS: the `fips` feature "enables support for FIPS140-3-approved cryptography, via the aws-lc-rs crate", changes the `require_ems` default, and the manual cites "FIPS 140-3 certificate #4816"; runtime check via `ServerConfig::fips()`, which "also covers TLS-level configuration that NIST recommends". FIPS builds "always require CMake and Go in addition to a C/C++ compiler" and on Windows also Ninja, and "will result in the creation of shared libraries" (aws-lc-rs platform and Windows pages). Pre-generated FIPS bindings exist only for the six Linux and macOS x86_64 and aarch64 targets.

Provider build requirements: non-FIPS aws-lc-rs: "CMake is never required", "Bindgen is never required (pre-generated bindings are provided)", a C/C++ compiler is needed, and "NASM is required for x86 and x86-64 builds on Windows" unless the `prebuilt-nasm` feature or `AWS_LC_SYS_PREBUILT_NASM=1` is used (objects "only available for Windows platforms"). The measured graph still lists the `cmake` crate as a build dependency of aws-lc-sys even for non-FIPS; that is a crate, not the CMake tool, and matches "never required" at the tool level. ring: build dep `cc ^1.2.8` only.

Provider recommendation: default to aws-lc-rs on the tier-one server targets (Linux x86_64 and aarch64 gnu and musl, macOS, Windows MSVC) because it is rustls's default, carries the post-quantum group ("X25519MLKEM768 is available when using the aws-lc-rs provider", Defaults manual), the FIPS path, and formal verification on parts of the primitives; offer `ring` as the feature for no_std, wasm, and toolchain-constrained builds (no NASM, no C++), which is what pamoja-mqtt already does. Do not install a provider implicitly in the library crate: `CryptoProvider::install_default()` "can be called successfully at most once in any process execution", and "libraries should rely on the default provider, while applications should call install_default() early". The zero-server core is a library loaded into Node, Python, and .NET hosts, so it must accept an `Arc<CryptoProvider>` through `builder_with_provider` (or `builder_with_details`) and never call `install_default()` itself; only the standalone binary does. Keep graviola on the watch list, not the allowlist, until it stops describing itself as "very new"; its architecture floor (x86_64 with avx2, adx, bmi2, pclmulqdq; aarch64 with aes, sha2, pmull, neon) also excludes older hardware.

Security posture of the stack (what the policy relies on): audit funded by CNCF at Buoyant.io's request and completed by Cure53 (rustls.dev blog; the report is `audit/TLS-01-report.pdf` in the repository); OSS-Fuzz registration; ISRG Prossimo funding; server-side handshake latency "roughly 2x lower than OpenSSL" and flat scaling to 80 Ampere cores (memorysafety.org, Rustls Server-Side Performance, 2025-05-13; no absolute handshake or memory-per-connection numbers are given there).

## 4. kTLS offload on Linux

Kernel facts (Documentation/networking/tls.rst and include/uapi/linux/tls.h):

- Enable with `setsockopt(sock, SOL_TCP, TCP_ULP, "tls", sizeof("tls"))` on an established TCP socket, then `TLS_TX` (1) and `TLS_RX` (2) with a `tls12_crypto_info_*` struct carrying key, IV, salt, and record sequence. "Currently only the symmetric encryption is handled in the kernel": the handshake stays in user space (rustls).
- Cipher constants: `TLS_CIPHER_AES_GCM_128 51`, `AES_GCM_256 52`, `AES_CCM_128 53`, `CHACHA20_POLY1305 54`, `SM4_GCM 55`, `SM4_CCM 56`, `ARIA_GCM_128 57`, `ARIA_GCM_256 58`; versions `TLS_1_2_VERSION` (3.3) and `TLS_1_3_VERSION` (3.4).
- RX: "A full TLS record must be received before decryption can happen." Control records (alerts, handshake) surface through a cmsg with `TLS_GET_RECORD_TYPE`; "an error is returned if a control message is received" and the caller supplied no cmsg buffer. TX of non-data records uses `TLS_SET_RECORD_TYPE`.
- TLS 1.3 key updates: "Decryption will be paused when a KeyUpdate message is received by the kernel, until the new key has been provided using the TLS_RX socket option" (doc commit "docs: tls: document TLS1.3 key updates", 2024-12-16). Statistics include `TlsTxRekeyOk` and `TlsRxRekeyReceived`, so rekey is a first-class path in current kernels.
- Optimizations: `TLS_TX_ZEROCOPY_RO` (3) "Allow sendfile() data to be transmitted directly to the NIC without making an in-kernel copy" (documented 2022-06-14); `TLS_RX_EXPECT_NO_PAD` (4), "TLS 1.3 only. Expect the sender to not pad records. This allows the data to be decrypted directly into user space buffers" (2022-07-06). `sendfile` "will send the file's data over TLS records of maximum length (2^14)". A 2025-10-27 doc commit adds "support setting the maximum payload size".
- Device offload (tls-offload.html): `TLS_SW` means "CPU handles the cryptography"; `TLS_HW` means "the NIC handles crypto on a packet by packet basis, provided the packets arrive in order"; "Offload does not currently support TLS 1.3"; it requires checksum offload; it "will not offload sockets routed through software interfaces such as those used for tunneling". `TLS_CONF_HW_RECORD` is marked "unused" in the uapi header.

rustls side: `ServerConfig::enable_secret_extraction` "Allows traffic secrets to be extracted after the handshake, e.g. for kTLS setup"; `ServerConnection::dangerous_extract_secrets()` returns `ExtractedSecrets` and "Should be used with care as it exposes secret key material"; `ConnectionTrafficSecrets` is `#[non_exhaustive]` with `Aes128Gcm`, `Aes256Gcm`, and `Chacha20Poly1305`, each `{ key: AeadKey, iv: Iv }`, and "can be used to configure kTLS for a socket in one direction". Those three suites map one to one onto kernel constants 51, 52, 54.

ktls crate (docs.rs): "Configures kTLS for tokio-rustls client and server connections", depends on `rustls ^0.23.12` and `tokio-rustls ^0.26.0`, targets `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, wraps the socket in `CorkStream` because it "is the only way to drain a rustls stream cleanly" (reads record headers to stop at a message boundary before handing the fd to the kernel), signature `config_ktls_server<IO>(stream: TlsStream<CorkStream<IO>>) -> Result<KtlsStream<IO>, Error>`; the docs admit "I'm not clear how rekeying is handled" and only 25.53% of the crate is documented. Error variants: `UlpError`, `KtlsCompatibility`, `ExportSecrets`, `TlsCryptoInfoError`, `DrainError`, `NoNegotiatedCipherSuite`.

Recommendation: implement kTLS in house rather than adding the ktls crate. The work is three `setsockopt` calls plus the drain-at-record-boundary logic and cmsg handling, all of which sit on `libc`-level calls the core already needs for its own non-blocking I/O, and the crate's own documentation leaves TLS 1.3 rekey open. Rules: Linux only, opt-in per listener (`tls.ktls = "auto" | "off"`), only after the handshake completes and only for AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 sessions; refuse (fall back to user-space records) when `TCP_ULP` fails, when the negotiated suite is not one of the three, or when the socket is not a plain TCP socket; when a control record arrives on RX (cmsg type not application data), hand the bytes back to rustls to process the alert or KeyUpdate and reinstall keys with `TLS_RX`; use `TLS_TX_ZEROCOPY_RO` only for static-file `sendfile` paths; never enable `TLS_RX_EXPECT_NO_PAD` unless the peer is known not to pad (it is an optimization with a documented counter for violations). The `enable_secret_extraction` flag must be set only on configs used by listeners that opted in, so the default `ServerConfig` never exposes `dangerous_extract_secrets`. Do not plan around NIC offload: TLS 1.3 is excluded there today.

## 5. Certificate handling, ALPN, resumption, OCSP, defaults

Certificates and keys: load PEM through `rustls_pki_types::pem::PemObject` (the `pem` module needs the `alloc` feature); `CertificateDer`, `PrivateKeyDer` (PKCS#8, PKCS#1, SEC1). `with_single_cert(cert_chain, key_der)` builds a static identity; "The commonName field is disregarded" in favor of subjectAltName. For reloads and SNI, implement `ResolvesServerCert`: `fn resolve(&self, client_hello: ClientHello<'_>) -> Option<Arc<CertifiedKey>>`, "Return None to abort the handshake"; `ClientHello::server_name()` returns the SNI or None; `CertifiedKey::from_der` verifies the key matches the end-entity certificate ("keys_match ... comparison of SubjectPublicKeyInfo bytes"). Hold the current `Arc<CertifiedKey>` per hostname behind a lock-free swap so a reload never blocks a handshake, and reject a reload whose `keys_match()` fails. Unknown SNI: return the default identity rather than aborting, matching what Node's `https.createServer` does today (unverified as a documented Node behavior; it is how zero-server behaves in `lib/app.js` by passing one cert).

ALPN: `alpn_protocols` is "Protocol names we support, most preferred first. If empty we don't do ALPN at all"; the server "selects its preferred protocol from the set submitted by the client" (`ClientHello::alpn()`). RFC 7301 section 3.2: "the server SHOULD select the most highly preferred protocol that it supports and that is also advertised by the client" and "In the event that the server supports no protocols that the client advertises, then the server SHALL respond with a fatal no_application_protocol alert". RFC 9325 section 3.8 makes ALPN support a MUST. zero-server's STANDARDS.md already records statements 13 to 15 (h2 over TLS 1.2+, most preferred protocol, fatal alert on no overlap, 0-RTT disabled); keep them as acceptance tests. Default `alpn_protocols = ["h2", "http/1.1"]` when HTTP/2 is enabled, `["http/1.1"]` otherwise. Correction to the first run: `ignore_client_order` is about cipher suites, not ALPN ("Ignore the client's ciphersuite order. Instead, choose the top ciphersuite in the server list which is supported by the client", ServerConfig docs). ALPN ordering needs no flag: the selection code in `rustls/src/server/hs.rs` iterates the server's list and picks the first entry the client also offered (`our_protocols.iter().find(|ours| their_protocols.iter().any(...))`), so the server's preference always wins. The same code returns `Error::NoApplicationProtocol` when the client offered protocols, the server list is non-empty, and nothing matched; a client that sends no ALPN extension at all proceeds without ALPN over TCP. For QUIC the check is stricter: `if chosen_protocol.is_none() && (!our_protocols.is_empty() || hello.protocols.is_some()) { return Err(Error::NoApplicationProtocol) }`, which is what RFC 9001 section 8.1 demands. The conformance test still asserts the wire alert (`no_application_protocol`, RFC 7301 section 3.2) since the fetched code shows the error, not the alert encoding.

Resumption: rustls defaults (std) store "256 sessions in memory" (`ServerSessionMemoryCache::new(size)`, "may be rounded-up for efficiency"), send `send_tls13_tickets = 2`, and `max_early_data_size = 0` so 0-RTT is off. `Ticketer::new()` (aws_lc_rs) "produces tickets with a 12 hour life and randomly generated keys" using "RFC 5077 section 4 Recommended Ticket Construction, using AES 256 for encryption and HMAC-SHA256"; `TicketRotator::new(lifetime, generator)`: "lifetime is in seconds, and is how long the current ticketer is used to generate new tickets. Tickets are accepted for no longer than twice this duration." `ProducesTickets::lifetime()` "must be implemented by key rolling and erasure, not by storing a lifetime in the ticket", and `decrypt` input "is fully attacker controlled, so this decryption must be side-channel free, panic-proof". RFC 9325 section 3.4: "Ticket-encryption keys MUST be changed regularly" and validity "MUST be limited to a reasonable duration"; RFC 8446 section 4.6.1 caps ticket_lifetime at 604800 seconds. Defaults to ship: tickets on, `TicketRotator` with a 6 hour lifetime (12 hour acceptance window), session cache sized by a `tls.session_cache` setting (256 default, 0 to disable and save memory per idle client), `ignore_client_order = true`, 0-RTT off and not exposed in the first release (RFC 8446 section 8 replay mitigations need single-use tickets or ClientHello recording, and section 2.3 says 0-RTT data "is not forward secret"). Multi-process deployments need one ticket key across workers; that is a custom `ProducesTickets` seeded from a shared secret, which the `ProducesTickets` trait makes possible without patching rustls.

OCSP stapling: rustls staples whatever DER response it is given ("ocsp is a DER-encoded OCSP response. Ignored if zero length"; `CertifiedKey.ocsp: Option<Vec<u8>>`, "An optional OCSP response from the certificate issuer, attesting to its continued validity"). It does not fetch. RFC 6066 section 8: the server "MAY also choose not to send a CertificateStatus message" and "Only one OCSP response may be sent". RFC 6960 Appendix A: POST with `Content-Type: application/ocsp-request` and the DER `OCSPRequest` body, or GET with the base64 URL form for requests under 255 bytes; section 4.2.2.1: responses whose `nextUpdate` is earlier than local time or whose `thisUpdate` is in the future "SHOULD be considered unreliable". RFC 7633: certificates carrying `id-pe-tlsfeature` (id-pe 24) with status_request make the staple mandatory, and a client "SHOULD reject the TLS configuration" without it. Design: a stapler task per identity that reads the AIA OCSP URL from the certificate, POSTs the request with the core's own HTTP client, validates `thisUpdate`/`nextUpdate`, swaps the `CertifiedKey` with the new `ocsp` bytes, refreshes at half the remaining interval, keeps serving the last good staple on fetch failure, and exposes `tls.ocsp_stapling = "auto" | "file:<path>" | "off"`. Building the OCSPRequest needs a small DER encoder for issuer name hash, issuer key hash, and serial; that is in-house code (no x509 crate on the allowlist), and the certificate parsing needed for AIA and serial is the same minimal DER walker. Must-staple certificates default to `auto` and refuse to start with `off`.

Client authentication (mTLS, optional): `WebPkiClientVerifier` "uses the webpki crate to perform client certificate validation" against provided roots, with `with_crls` and `allow_unauthenticated` for optional client certs; `with_no_client_auth()` otherwise. Revocation policy knobs beyond CRLs were not in the fetched page.

Secure defaults (the shipped `ServerConfig`, all traceable):

| Setting | Default | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Protocol versions | TLS 1.3 and 1.2 (`with_safe_default_protocol_versions`) | rustls ConfigBuilder; RFC 9325 3.1.1 (1.2 MUST, 1.3 SHOULD and MUST be preferred; 1.0/1.1 MUST NOT) |
| Cipher suites | provider defaults, AES-256-GCM preferred, then AES-128-GCM, ChaCha20; AEAD and ECDHE only | rustls Defaults manual; RFC 9325 4.1 and 4.2 |
| Key exchange | X25519MLKEM768 first with aws-lc-rs (`prefer-post-quantum` is a default feature), X25519 before P-256 | rustls Defaults manual and features page |
| `require_ems` | false unless FIPS; expose `tls.require_ems = true` for strict deployments | ServerConfig docs; RFC 9325 3.5 (MUST support) |
| `max_early_data_size` | 0 | ServerConfig docs; RFC 8446 8 |
| `send_half_rtt_data` | false | ServerConfig docs |
| `max_fragment_size` | None (16 KB records) | ServerConfig docs |
| `alpn_protocols` | h2, http/1.1 | RFC 7301, RFC 9325 3.8 |
| `ignore_client_order` (cipher suite order) | true, so the provider's AES-256-GCM first ordering wins over the client's | ServerConfig docs |
| Tickets | TicketRotator, 6 h generation, 12 h acceptance, keys in memory only | rustls ticketer docs; RFC 9325 3.4; RFC 8446 4.6.1 |
| Session cache | 256 entries, configurable | ServerConfig docs |
| Certificate compression | off (no brotli or zlib crates) | rustls features page |
| `enable_secret_extraction` | false unless the listener opts into kTLS | ServerConfig docs |
| `logging` feature | off in release builds (drops the `log` crate) | rustls features page |
| Crypto provider | supplied by the host, never `install_default()` from the library | CryptoProvider docs |

## 6. Dependency policy proposal

### 6.1 Allowlist (the only third-party crates the shipped graph may contain)

| Crate | Why it is allowed | Constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rustls (0.23.x; 0.24 when released) | the TLS engine; audited, fuzzed, advisory pipeline, no legacy protocol surface | `default-features = false`; features chosen per target: `std`, `tls12`, provider; `logging` only in dev profiles |
| rustls-webpki, rustls-pki-types, untrusted, subtle, zeroize, once_cell | hard dependencies of rustls; webpki does path validation and CRLs; subtle and zeroize give constant-time comparison and key erasure | follow rustls's own version bounds; never depended on directly except pki-types for the public certificate types |
| aws-lc-rs and aws-lc-sys (0.24: rustls-aws-lc-rs) | default provider, post-quantum group, FIPS option, formally verified primitives | non-FIPS only by default; `prebuilt-nasm` on Windows CI; FIPS behind a separate feature that is never on in bindings |
| ring (0.24: rustls-ring) | provider for no_std, wasm, and toolchains without C++ or NASM | optional feature; the README's "experiment" wording is why it is not the default |
| getrandom, libc, cfg-if | transitive provider needs (system entropy, syscalls) | libc is also the natural home for the kTLS `setsockopt` calls; no `nix` or `socket2` |
| cc, shlex, find-msvc-tools, cmake, dunce, fs_extra, jobserver | build-script helpers pulled by the providers | only under `build.allow-build-scripts` for aws-lc-sys and ring; nothing else in the workspace may have a build script |
| tokio, tokio-rustls, pin-project-lite | only if the async boundary uses tokio; otherwise excluded | decision belongs to the I/O research task; rustls's unbuffered API works with a custom epoll or io_uring loop without tokio-rustls |
| napi, napi-derive, napi-build, napi-sys (Node binding only) | Node-API ABI stability across Node releases | `default-features = false`, lowest Node-API level that carries what the binding needs (pamoja uses napi6 for BigInt); `tokio_rt` only if the binding schedules async work on a runtime |
| pyo3, pyo3-ffi, pyo3-build-config, pyo3-macros (Python binding only) | stable ABI wheels ("An abi3-py310 wheel supports all GIL-enabled CPython versions from Python 3.10 and newer", maturin) | `abi3-py3XX`; skip pyo3-async-runtimes and pyo3-stub-gen unless the stub generator is kept as a dev-only tool |
| cbindgen (.NET and C, build only) | generates the header the P/Invoke layer mirrors | MPL-2.0 exception as in pamoja; `default-features = false` |
| proc-macro2, quote, syn, unicode-ident, heck, target-lexicon, convert_case, semver, libloading, memchr, futures-* family, ctor, bitflags, nohash-hasher, rustc-hash, slab | transitive dependencies of napi and pyo3 as measured today | allowed only in the binding manifests, never in `crates/` |

Everything else is denied by construction: with `[bans] allow` populated, "any crate not in that list will be denied" (cargo-deny bans config). Candidates that stay off the list with the reason: `rustls-native-certs` and `webpki-roots` (a server does not verify peers unless mTLS or upstream TLS is enabled; add behind a feature only then, noting webpki-roots's CDLA-Permissive-2.0 license), `rcgen` (dev-only for test certificates, excluded by `exclude-dev`), `instant-acme` (Apache-2.0, pulls hyper, hyper-rustls, hyper-util; ACME belongs in an optional companion crate, not the core), `ktls` (in-house instead, section 4), `brotli`/`zlib-rs` (RFC 8879 is optional and adds compression code to the attack surface), `log`/`tracing` (the core has its own observability surface), `x509-parser`/`der` (the minimal DER walking for AIA, serial, and OCSP is written in house).

### 6.2 cargo-deny (`deny.toml`, extending pamoja's)

- `[graph] exclude-dev = true` as today. Run the check once per manifest: workspace, `bindings/node`, `bindings/python/packages/native` (cargo-deny reads one graph per run; pamoja's CI already loops clippy per manifest the same way).
- `[advisories]`: `yanked = "deny"`, `unmaintained = "workspace"` at minimum, every `ignore` with a `reason` and a review date in the note (advisories "now emit errors" and cannot be demoted, only ignored).
- `[licenses] allow` as pamoja; verified on 2026-09-30 that aws-lc-sys (`ISC AND (Apache-2.0 OR ISC) AND Apache-2.0 AND MIT AND BSD-3-Clause AND ...`), ring (`Apache-2.0 AND ISC`), and rustls-webpki (`ISC`) are satisfied by that list with no exception. The only exception stays cbindgen (MPL-2.0, build only). If the `http3` feature lands with quinn-proto (section 8), its graph is MIT OR Apache-2.0 at the top and must be re-run through `cargo deny check licenses` before the allowlist is extended.
- `[bans]`: `allow = [...]` the table above, `multiple-versions = "deny"` (pamoja uses warn; the measured graphs already have a getrandom 0.2 versus 0.4 split between ring and aws-lc-rs, so pick one provider per build to keep it clean), `wildcards = "deny"`, `external-default-features = "deny"` so every third-party crate is consumed with `default-features = false`, `features` entries denying `rustls/logging` in release and `napi/serde-json` and similar, `build.allow-build-scripts = [aws-lc-sys, ring, napi-build, pyo3-build-config, cbindgen consumers]`, `build.executables = "deny"`.
- `[sources]`: `unknown-registry = "deny"`, `unknown-git = "deny"`, no `allow-git` (a git dependency means a fork, and forks go through `[patch]` plus a tracked upstream issue, never into a release).

### 6.3 cargo-vet and cargo-audit: use both, for different questions

- cargo-deny's advisories check already queries the RustSec database, so `cargo audit` on the source tree is redundant in CI. Its value is `cargo audit bin` on shipped artifacts: "If your programs have been compiled with cargo auditable, the audit is fully accurate because all the necessary information is embedded in the compiled binary". `cargo auditable build --release` embeds a zlib-compressed JSON dependency list in a `.dep-v0` linker section, "under 4kB even on large dependency trees with 400+ entries", and cargo audit 0.17.3+, trivy 0.31+, grype 0.83+, and osv-scanner 2.0.1+ read it. Build every cdylib shipped to npm, PyPI, and NuGet with `cargo auditable` so a downstream scanner can see rustls and aws-lc-sys versions inside the native module.
- cargo-vet answers the question cargo-deny cannot: has a human read this code? It "matches all of a project's third-party dependencies against a set of audits performed by the project authors or entities they trust", with sharing, relative (diff) audits, and an exemptions list that "can be ratcheted down over time". Import the registry sets that cover this graph: `mozilla`, `google`, `bytecode-alliance`, `isrg`, `embark-studios`, `zcash` (all in the cargo-vet `registry.toml`); imports are "not transitive". Use `cargo vet trust` only for the rustls organization's crates and only with an expiration ("Entries require a trust expiration date"), since trust "is fundamentally a heuristic". Run `cargo vet` in CI beside `cargo deny check`; a new dependency lands in `exemptions` only with a review date, and the exemptions count is reported on every release.

### 6.4 Vendoring and lock discipline

- Commit `Cargo.lock` in the workspace and in each binding crate (pamoja already commits both binding lockfiles) and build everything with `--locked`, which "Asserts that the exact same dependencies and versions are used as when the existing Cargo.lock file was originally generated" and is meant for "environments where deterministic builds are desired, such as in CI pipelines". Release builds use `--frozen` ("Equivalent to specifying both --locked and --offline") after a `cargo fetch` step, so a registry outage or a yanked crate cannot change a release.
- Vendoring: `cargo vendor --versioned-dirs --locked vendor/` plus the printed `[source.crates-io] replace-with = "vendored-sources"` and `[source.vendored-sources] directory = "vendor"` block in `.cargo/config.toml`; Cargo "treats vendored sources as read-only". Because aws-lc-sys alone is 67 MB of source, do not commit the vendor directory to the repository; produce the vendor tarball as a release artifact (attached to the GitHub release next to the crates) so an offline rebuild of any tag is possible, and keep the repository at the size of the lockfile.

### 6.5 Reproducible builds

- Pin the toolchain to an exact version in `rust-toolchain.toml` (pamoja floats on `stable`) and pin the Docker image by digest for the fmt, clippy, and release jobs.
- Paths: `--remap-path-prefix FROM=TO` rewrites path prefixes "in all output, including compiler diagnostics, debug information, macro expansions"; `--remap-path-scope` selects `macro`, `diagnostics`, `debuginfo`, `coverage`, `object`, or `all`. Cargo's profile `trim-paths` is still unstable (needs `cargo-features = ["trim-paths"]` or `-Z trim-paths`), so pass `--remap-path-prefix=$PWD=/src` and `--remap-path-prefix=$CARGO_HOME=/cargo` through `RUSTFLAGS` in release jobs. The C objects from aws-lc-sys and ring need the equivalent flag through the C compiler; Cargo documents `CARGO_TRIM_PATHS_REMAP` for build scripts to forward "via cc's -ffile-prefix-map", but that variable is only set when the unstable `trim-paths` is active, so on stable the C side needs `CFLAGS=-ffile-prefix-map=...`. The cc crate documents that it reads `CFLAGS` ("a series of space separated flags passed to compilers"), with `CFLAGS_<target>` and `TARGET_CFLAGS` taking priority, and that `CRATE_CC_NO_DEFAULTS` disables its default flag set; so the variable reaches the compiler for ring and aws-lc-sys objects. Whether the resulting objects are byte-identical across build roots is what the two-build hash check below proves.
- Set `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` (seconds since the Unix epoch, "a standardised environment variable that distributions can set centrally") to the commit timestamp for release jobs so anything timestamp-sensitive in build scripts, packaging, and the NuGet or wheel archives lines up.
- Keep `codegen-units = 1` and `lto = "thin"` as pamoja does; add a CI job that builds the release cdylib twice in separate containers and fails when the SHA-256 differs, which is the only way to prove the above rather than assert it.

### 6.6 How the bindings keep their own dependency sets minimal

- The bindings never depend on rustls, a crypto provider, or tokio-rustls directly; they consume the core crate through its Rust API (Node, Python) or its C ABI (.NET, C, C++). TLS, kTLS, and OCSP are Cargo features of the core, so a binding that ships without TLS (for example a Python package used only for the codec layer) carries none of the provider source.
- Node: `napi` with `default-features = false` and the lowest `napiN` feature that carries the needed types; no `serde-json`, `chrono`, `anyhow`; JavaScript-side conversion happens in TypeScript. Platform packages under `optionalDependencies` with `os`, `cpu`, and `libc` fields, as the napi-rs getting-started documents.
- Python: `pyo3` with one `abi3-py3XX` feature so maturin emits one wheel per platform ("maturin will choose at most one stable ABI family for the build"); the `extension-module` feature is "Deprecated, users should remove this feature and upgrade to maturin >= 1.9.4". Keep pyo3-stub-gen as a dev tool that is not part of the wheel graph.
- .NET: the ffi crate keeps a curated `extern "C"` surface, cbindgen at build time only (MPL-2.0 exception), the cdylib packed per runtime identifier; no NuGet-side dependency beyond the runtime.
- Each binding has its own `Cargo.lock`, its own `cargo deny check --manifest-path`, its own `cargo vet` (or the workspace's supply-chain directory with the binding manifest included), and is built with `cargo auditable`.

## 7. What transfers from the existing zero-server

- `docs/STANDARDS.md` already carries verified statements for ALPN selection and the `no_application_protocol` alert (RFC 7301 section 3.2), h2 over TLS 1.2+ (RFC 9113 section 9.2), and 0-RTT disabled (RFC 8446 section 8), with RFC 7301, RFC 8446, and RFC 9525 recorded as verified sources on 2026-09-28. These become the TLS conformance vectors of the Rust core unchanged.
- `lib/app.js` shows the current surface: `http2.createSecureServer` with `allowHTTP1` defaulting to true and `https.createServer` for HTTP/1.1; `lib/fetch/index.js` exposes `ciphers`, `minVersion`, `maxVersion`, `servername`. The Rust configuration keys should mirror these names so the Node binding keeps the existing option shape (`allowHTTP1` maps to the ALPN list, `minVersion` to the protocol version set).
- Nothing about Node's OpenSSL-backed session cache or ticket keys transfers; the rustls ticket and cache design in section 5 replaces it.

## 8. HTTP/3 and QUIC head start: what changes for TLS and for the dependency policy

The owner asked for an early position on HTTP/3. This section covers only the TLS and dependency consequences; the transport design belongs to the HTTP and I/O research tasks.

### 8.1 What the RFCs fix in place

- RFC 9114 section 3.1: HTTP/3 is identified by the ALPN token `"h3"`; "Servers MAY serve HTTP/3 on any UDP port; an alternative service advertisement always includes an explicit port"; the client "MUST verify that the certificate is an acceptable match for the URI's origin server". Section 3.1.1: an origin advertises HTTP/3 through `Alt-Svc`, for example `Alt-Svc: h3=":50781"`, so the HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 responders must be able to emit that header. Section 2: "HTTP/3 replaces HPACK with QPACK" because HPACK "relies on in-order transmission of compressed field sections (a guarantee not provided by QUIC)". Section 3.2: "QUIC version 1 uses TLS version 1.3 or greater as its handshake protocol".
- RFC 9001 section 4.2: "An endpoint MUST terminate the connection if a version of TLS older than 1.3 is negotiated". Section 4: handshake messages are "carried directly over the QUIC transport" in CRYPTO frames, not TLS records. Section 8.1: "endpoints MUST use ALPN", failure closes with `0x0178` (no_application_protocol). Section 8.2: "Endpoints MUST send the quic_transport_parameters extension". Section 5.4: header protection with a separate "quic hp" key. Section 5.6: 0-RTT only when "specifically requested by the application". Section 6: endpoints "MUST NOT send a TLS KeyUpdate message"; QUIC's own key update replaces it.
- RFC 9000 section 8.1: before address validation "an endpoint MUST NOT send more than three times as much data as it has received", and "a server uses a Retry packet to perform address validation". Section 14.1: Initial datagrams are padded to at least 1200 bytes.

### 8.2 rustls already carries the QUIC TLS surface (no new TLS dependency)

`rustls::quic` ("APIs for implementing QUIC TLS") provides `ServerConnection::new(config: Arc<ServerConfig>, quic_version: Version, params: Vec<u8>)`, where `params` is "the TLS-encoded transport parameters to send"; `read_hs(&mut self, plaintext: &[u8])` ("Handshake data obtained from separate encryption levels should be supplied in separate calls"); `write_hs(&mut self, buf: &mut [Vec<u8>]) -> Option<KeyChange>` ("When this returns Some(_), the new keys must be used for future handshake data"); `KeyChange::Handshake { keys }` and `KeyChange::OneRtt { keys, next: Secrets }` where `next` holds "Secrets to derive updated keys from" and "only packet keys are updated by key updates; header protection keys remain the same"; `zero_rtt_keys()`, `alert()` ("Check after read_hs returns Err(_)"), `quic_transport_parameters()` for the peer's parameters, `reject_early_data()`, `alpn_protocol()`, `negotiated_cipher_suite()`, `server_name()`. `Version` has `V1Draft` ("Draft versions 29, 30, 31 and 32"), `V1` ("First stable RFC"), and `V2` ("Anti-ossification variant of V1"). The `PacketKey`, `HeaderProtectionKey`, and `Algorithm` traits plus `Suite` produce the packet protection keys from the negotiated TLS 1.3 suite, so the AEAD work stays inside the crypto provider.

Consequences for this document's policy:

- The TLS allowlist does not grow for HTTP/3. The same rustls crate, provider, webpki, and pki-types serve TCP and QUIC; the same `ResolvesServerCert`, ticketer, session cache, and OCSP staple feed both. One `ServerConfig` can be shared, with `alpn_protocols` extended by `h3` on the QUIC listener only.
- `rustls::quic::ServerConnection`, `ClientConnection`, and `Connection` are marked "Available on crate feature std only", so a no_std QUIC handshake through rustls is not available today; the no_std scope in the design stays at codecs and the HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 framing, and QUIC lives in the std-enabled I/O crate.
- kTLS does not apply. It is a TCP ULP (`setsockopt(SOL_TCP, TCP_ULP, "tls")`, section 4); QUIC packet protection runs in user space through the `PacketKey` trait. The Linux fast path for QUIC is instead `UDP_SEGMENT` ("since Linux 4.18", "Enables UDP segmentation offload ... transferring multiple datagrams worth of data as a single large packet through the kernel transmit path, even when that exceeds MTU") and `UDP_GRO` ("since Linux 5.0", "the socket may receive multiple datagrams worth of data as a single large buffer, together with a cmsg(3) that holds the segment size"), plus ECN marking, which the kernel segmentation document describes as `SKB_GSO_UDP_L4` advertised through `NETIF_F_GSO_UDP_L4`. These are `libc`-level `setsockopt` and `sendmsg`/`recvmsg` cmsg calls, the same class as the kTLS work, so they fit the in-house I/O layer with no new crate.
- The secure defaults extend naturally: TLS 1.3 only on the QUIC listener (RFC 9001 4.2), `max_early_data_size = 0` (0-RTT stays off, RFC 9001 5.6 and RFC 8446 8), ALPN list non-empty so rustls's stricter QUIC check (section 5, hs.rs) rejects a client without a matching protocol, the 3x amplification limit and Retry under load (RFC 9000 8.1), 1200-byte Initial padding (RFC 9000 14.1), and QUIC key update driven from `Secrets` rather than TLS KeyUpdate (RFC 9001 6).

### 8.3 The transport: measured options and their dependency cost

| Option | License | Shape | Direct runtime crates | Notes from the fetched pages |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| quinn-proto 0.11.18 (2026-09-14) | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | "performs no I/O whatsoever" (`Endpoint::handle` consumes datagrams with timestamp, remote, local IP, ECN, bytes; `accept`, `refuse`, `retry` when `may_retry()`; caller drives sockets and timers) | bytes, lru-slab, rand, rand_pcg, rustc-hash, slab, thiserror, tinyvec, tracing, getrandom 0.4, rustls-pki-types, web-time (12, all non-optional; tracing is mandatory, the `log` feature only toggles its log bridge); optional rustls, ring, aws-lc-rs, rustls-platform-verifier, qlog, fastbloom, arbitrary | defaults are `bloom`, `log`, `rustls-ring`, `ring`; select `default-features = false, features = ["rustls-aws-lc-rs"]` to stay on one provider (the `aws-lc-rs` feature also turns on aws-lc-rs `prebuilt-nasm`); `crypto` module traits `Session`, `ServerConfig`, `ClientConfig`, `PacketKey`, `HeaderKey`, `HandshakeTokenKey`, `HmacKey`, `AeadKey`, `KeyPair`, `Keys` allow a custom TLS or in-house provider; workspace MSRV 1.80.0 with releases "at least 6 months old"; 1.2 MB source |
| quinn 0.11.12 (async wrapper) | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | tokio-based; 20 features, defaults `bloom`, `log`, `platform-verifier`, `runtime-tokio`, `rustls-ring` | adds tokio, quinn-udp (libc, socket2, windows-sys; "Segmentation offload for bulk send and receive operations, reducing CPU load", ECN, IP fragmentation disabled), plus quinn-proto's set | only needed if the async boundary is tokio; the sans-IO quinn-proto is the fit for an in-house epoll or io_uring loop |
| quiche 0.30.0 (2026-09-17) | BSD-2-Clause | Cloudflare; BoringSSL through boring-sys | bytes, debug_panic, either, enum_dispatch, intrusive-collections, libc, libm, log, octets, slab, smallvec, windows-sys; optional boring, boring-sys, qlog, serde, serde_json, serde_with, sfv | boring-sys "requires the cmake command to be available during the build process" and "NASM is also required" on Windows; a second crypto library next to aws-lc-rs, so excluded |
| s2n-quic 1.89.0 (2026-09-22) | Apache-2.0 | AWS; "s2n-tls is used as the default TLS provider" on unix and MinGW, rustls on Windows MSVC | bytes, cfg-if, futures, rand, tokio plus `=0.89.0` pinned s2n-codec, s2n-quic-core, s2n-quic-platform, s2n-quic-transport; optional s2n-quic-rustls, s2n-quic-tls, zerocopy, zeroize | tokio and futures mandatory; the s2n-tls default is a C library the policy would have to vet in addition to AWS-LC; excluded |
| h3 0.0.8 (2025-05-06) | MIT | HTTP/3 framing generic over a QUIC transport | bytes, fastrand, futures-util, http, pin-project-lite, tokio; optional tracing | pre-1.0, tokio mandatory, and the `http` crate would duplicate the core's own header and status types; excluded, HTTP/3 framing and QPACK are in-house like HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 |
| In-house QUIC over `rustls::quic` | none | RFC 9000 transport, RFC 9002 loss detection and congestion control (not fetched in this task), RFC 9114 framing, RFC 9204 QPACK (not fetched) | none beyond the TLS set | matches the zero-third-party rule for non-TLS code, largest engineering cost |

Recommendation for the head start (no transport commitment yet):

1. Design the UDP path of the I/O layer now with `UDP_SEGMENT`, `UDP_GRO`, ECN cmsgs, and `IP_PMTUDISC_DO` style fragmentation control as first-class calls next to the kTLS `setsockopt` work, on the `libc` crate the policy already allows. That work is needed whichever QUIC transport lands.
2. Make the HTTP semantics layer (method, target, headers, status, body streams, trailers) transport-agnostic from the first commit so HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 share it; HTTP/3 then adds only framing and QPACK. Write QPACK's static table and the encoder and decoder as no_std in-house code with conformance vectors; it is independent of TLS and of the transport choice, and RFC 9204 must be fetched and recorded in STANDARDS.md when that starts.
3. Give the HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 responders an `Alt-Svc` emission hook (`h3=":<port>"`, RFC 9114 3.1.1) behind the `http3` feature so upgrade is a configuration change.
4. Shape the internal TLS seam around `rustls::quic::ServerConnection`'s three calls (`read_hs`, `write_hs` with `KeyChange`, `quic_transport_parameters`) so the QUIC transport, in-house or quinn-proto, plugs into the same certificate resolver, ticketer, and staple as TCP.
5. If time to market decides, quinn-proto with `default-features = false, features = ["rustls-aws-lc-rs"]` is the only candidate compatible with the single-provider rule and the sans-IO loop. It carries 12 mandatory crates including `tracing`, so it goes behind an off-by-default `http3` feature with its own allowlist addendum in `deny.toml` and is never on by default in the bindings. Whether `tracing` is acceptable in the shipped graph is an owner decision; the in-house path is the only one with zero additions.
6. Node context: `node:quic` is "Stability: 1.0 - Early development", added in v23.8.0, requires `--experimental-quic`, and "only supports HTTP/3 as a built-in application protocol". The Node binding of the Rust core would therefore ship HTTP/3 on stable Node releases that have none, which is a differentiator for the existing `@zero-server/sdk` users; the binding must own the UDP socket, as it already must for kTLS.

## 9. Risks

- HTTP/3 doubles the transport surface: QUIC is user-space packet protection with no kernel offload, and RFC 9000 address validation, amplification limits, and key update are correctness-critical; an in-house transport has no advisory pipeline, and quinn-proto adds twelve mandatory crates including `tracing`. The `http3` feature must stay off by default until conformance vectors cover RFC 9000, 9001, 9002, 9114, and 9204.
- rustls's QUIC connection types are std-only, so no_std cannot extend to the QUIC handshake.
- rustls 0.24 moves providers to separate crates; the allowlist and deny configuration must be re-cut on that upgrade, and every binding lockfile bumps together.
- aws-lc-sys is 67 MB of C source with a `cc` plus `cmake` build path; build time and the C toolchain requirement (NASM on Windows x86_64 unless `prebuilt-nasm`) land on every binding CI matrix.
- ring describes itself as "An experiment." and inherits BoringSSL's "not intended for general use" warning; as the no_std provider it needs a documented sunset plan if rustls-ring lags.
- kTLS is Linux only, TLS 1.3 rekey handling has to be implemented and tested in house (the ktls crate leaves it open), and NIC offload excludes TLS 1.3; a bug here leaks plaintext or hangs a connection, so it must stay opt-in with the fall-back path exercised in CI under a kernel that has the `tls` ULP module loaded.
- Two providers in one build split `getrandom` into 0.2 and 0.4 (measured), which `multiple-versions = "deny"` will flag; feature unification across bindings must be checked so no build carries both providers.
- OCSP stapling requires an outbound HTTP client and a DER encoder in the core; a must-staple certificate with a broken responder becomes an outage, so the "serve last good staple" and startup refusal rules must be tested.
- Reproducible builds depend on unstable Cargo path trimming; until `trim-paths` stabilizes the C objects may retain absolute paths, which the two-build hash check will expose.
- cargo-vet imports cover most of this graph but not necessarily aws-lc-sys at the pinned version; exemptions for the provider crates will exist on day one and need a named owner.

## 10. Unverified (not fetched or not measured in this task)

Resolved on 2026-09-30: SPDX strings for aws-lc-sys, ring, rustls-webpki (crates.io API); rustls's ALPN mismatch behavior (`hs.rs` returns `Error::NoApplicationProtocol`; the alert byte on the wire is still a conformance-test assertion); the cc crate reading `CFLAGS`.

- Kernel versions that introduced `TLS_TX`, `TLS_RX`, TLS 1.3 kTLS, and rekey (the kernel.org git log returned 403; only documentation commit dates from GitHub are cited).
- The ktls crate's kernel version floor, TLS 1.2 support, and maintenance status.
- The Cure53 finding count (the PDF could not be rendered locally; only the project blog's statement of the audit is cited).
- Node's behavior for unknown SNI without `SNICallback`.
- Any absolute kTLS throughput or CPU saving; no benchmark was run.
